entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Tufts University in Medford, Massachusetts, founded 1852 by Universalist clergy as the first liberal arts college established by the Universalist church — a denomination committed to universal salvation and religious tolerance — is now a major research university known for its Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy (1933, America's oldest graduate school of international affairs), the Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine, and a disproportionate record of producing foreign service officers, ambassadors, and international development leaders. The Fletcher School trained more US ambassadors per capita than any other institution.

The Universalist founders' commitment to non-sectarian education and racial inclusion was unusual for 1852: Tufts admitted its first African American student (Lewis Howard Latimer's father) before the Civil War, and the university never had racial admission restrictions. The founding on College Hill in Medford — on a hill donated by Charles Tufts, who described it as 'a light on a hill' — established a small New England liberal arts college.

The Fletcher School (1933), established during the interwar period as American global engagement expanded, trained diplomats and international lawyers at a time when international relations was barely recognized as an academic discipline. Fletcher alumni include multiple Secretaries of State, UN Ambassadors, and international organization heads. Tufts's School of Nutrition Science and Policy (1976) — the only such school in the US — made it the leading academic institution in global nutrition policy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tufts University's Fletcher School — America's oldest international affairs graduate school — trained a disproportionate share of US ambassadors and foreign service officers, making it one of America's most consequential diplomatic training institutions despite its relatively small size.
